item.text: {"question_id":"6B.10","answer":"By the end of the defined 2023 period, the supplied evidence supports a mixed and incompletely observed trajectory rather than a confirmed durable, population-wide improvement in life chances. Income and selected protections improved: multidimensional poverty fell from 41.9% in 2018 to 36.3% in 2022, labor poverty fell from 40.1% to 37.3% between the third quarters of 2022 and 2023, and real per-capita labor income rose 11.3% over that interval. Government transfers contributed materially in aggregate: CONEVAL estimated that without social transfers, 2022 poverty would have been 39.0% rather than 36.3%, although this is a statistical scenario covering federal, state, and municipal transfers and is not a complete causal estimate. The federal older-person pension expanded substantially, and older-person poverty and related income and security-social indicators improved between 2018 and 2022. However, these gains do not establish durable improvement for ordinary people as a whole or for disadvantaged groups. Extreme poverty was essentially unchanged in relative terms and increased from 8.7 to 9.1 million people; health-service deprivation rose from 16.2% to 39.1%, with especially severe increases among the poorest decile, rural residents, children, and people in extreme poverty. Education, social-security, food, and housing deficits persisted, while Indigenous people, children, people with disabilities, women in poverty, and rural communities remained disproportionately disadvantaged. Local progress coexisted with 7,136 high- or very-high-social-lag localities in 2020, including 5,258 with persistent lag, and program coverage was below the local poverty share in many municipalities. The 2023 labor gains also reflected post-pandemic recovery, domestic and external demand, nearshoring, remittances, and other factors; the hurricane response exposed serious short-term harms for poor residents in Acapulco. The evidence therefore supports genuine but uneven gains, with meaningful federal contribution in transfers, pensions, and wage policy, but substantial unresolved deprivation, distributional gaps, health-access deterioration, policy and measurement uncertainty, and no demonstrated durability beyond the
